title: Jekyll and Hyde: duality, secrecy, science and reputation
specPoints: Paper 1 Section B: the 19th-century novel, The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
AO1: themes and ideas; AO2: setting and imagery

tips.title: The chain of themes
tips.body: Reputation makes secrecy; secrecy makes duality; science gives it a body.

tips.title: Duality is everywhere
tips.body: The man, the building with two doors, the bright street and the foggy slum, the whole respectable society.

tips.title: Secrecy in the form
tips.body: The truth is written down, sealed and kept back until Chapters 9 and 10, as the gentlemen keep theirs.

tips.title: Setting is a method
tips.body: Fire in a forest; chocolate-coloured pall; drowned city; a tilted moon. Name what each does.

tips.title: Theme as a claim
tips.body: Duality is made by a society that forces a man to hide half of himself.

why.matters: Questions on this novel usually name an idea: fear, secrecy, duality, science, respectability. An answer that can turn the idea into a claim and show how it connects to the others, through the novel's setting and structure, is doing what the top level asks. The themes are also still alive: the gap between a public reputation and a private life, and the fear of what science might do to human nature, are arguments people still have.

examples.title: The respectable double life
examples.body: Stories of public figures with hidden lives recur in every generation's news. The pattern is Jekyll's: a reputation to protect, a private freedom, and discretion from friends who do not ask. The novel asks what that discretion costs.

examples.title: Science that changes what a person is
examples.body: Arguments about drugs that change mood or behaviour, and about what makes someone the same person, have the shape of Jekyll's experiment. Stevenson's version asks whether a person can be divided, and answers that the attempt destroys him.

steps.title: Duality: one man, truly two
steps.body:
The novel's central idea is stated in Jekyll's statement: “man is not truly one, but truly two” (Chapter 10). He had learned “the thorough and primitive duality of man”, and he calls it “that these incongruous faggots were thus bound together” (Chapter 10), bundles of sticks that do not belong together, “these polar twins should be continuously struggling”.

**Duality is everywhere, not only in Jekyll.** The building has two faces, a respectable front and a neglected back door. London has fine streets beside slums. Respectable men have secret lives. Even Utterson has a hidden taste: he drinks gin alone to mortify a taste for vintages.

**The twist in the idea.** Jekyll hoped to separate the two, so that the good could live without the evil. He failed because they were never equal halves: the drug was “neither diabolical nor divine” (Chapter 10), and it freed only the self he had shut up, “the brute that slept within me”.

check.prompt: Why does Jekyll call the good and evil in him incongruous faggots bound together?
check.solution: A faggot is a bundle of sticks. Incongruous means not matching. His image makes a person a bundle of things that do not fit, tied together, which is the curse of mankind he hopes to undo.

markScheme.description: They are like sticks bundled together that do not match, forced into one man

options: They are like sticks bundled together that do not match, forced into one man
Because he means that his body is made of wood and his servants have to keep him near the fire in winter, which is why he spends so much time in the cabinet with the fire lit
Because he is describing Hyde's walking stick
Because he is talking about his friends

steps.title: Secrecy: gentlemen who will not speak
steps.body:
**Silence as a code.** Enfield ends his story: “Let us make a bargain never to refer to this again” (Chapter 1). He will not ask about the name on the cheque: “the more it looks like Queer Street, the less I ask” (Chapter 1). He calls the house “Black Mail House”, and assumes the worst without asking.

**Documents kept shut.** Jekyll's will, Lanyon's envelope, the letters: each is sealed or locked away. Utterson puts Lanyon's envelope in his private safe unread.

**The novel's form is secret too.** The truth is written down and kept for the end, in the order that respectable men would release it. The June 2024 indicative content named the atmosphere of secrecy and the unknown throughout the novel.

Secrecy is not only something the characters do; it is what makes Hyde possible. A society in which gentlemen do not ask is a society in which Jekyll can keep a Hyde.

check.solution: Queer Street meant trouble, usually money trouble. Enfield's rule is gentlemanly discretion, and the novel shows its cost: the silence of respectable men is the space in which Hyde lives.

steps.title: Science: the mystic and the transcendental
steps.body:
**Two sciences.** Lanyon practises conventional, material medicine and calls Jekyll's work “unscientific balderdash”. Jekyll's studies led towards “the mystic and the transcendental”. In Chapter 9, as Hyde, he taunts Lanyon as a man “you who have denied the virtue of transcendental medicine”.

**Science that crosses a line.** Jekyll's experiment is not on a patient but on himself, and on the soul. The Victorian reader, living through rapid advances in medicine and in ideas about evolution, would feel the danger of a science that goes where religion said it should not.

**The proof kills the sceptic.** Lanyon sees the transformation and says “My life is shaken to its roots” (Chapter 9).

**The limit of control.** The experiment works only while the first supply of salt lasts, and that salt, Jekyll learns, was impure. His science succeeded by accident and fails by chance.

visuals.alt: A table comparing Lanyon's and Jekyll's science: their kind, their view of each other, and their outcome

check.prompt: What does the impure salt reveal about Jekyll's science?
check.solution: The first supply had an unknown impurity that made the drug work. When it runs out, no new supply succeeds, and Jekyll is trapped as Hyde. The scientist who meant to master his nature did not understand his own experiment.

markScheme.description: His success depended on an accident he never understood, so he never controlled what he made

options: That Jekyll was a poor chemist who bought cheap ingredients from a shop in Soho to save money, and the police traced the salt back to Hyde's rooms after the murder of Carew
That Poole poisoned the salt
His success depended on an accident he never understood, so he never controlled what he made
That the drug never worked

steps.title: Reputation: the name that must be saved
steps.body:
**Jekyll's motive.** He wanted pleasures that his standing would not allow, and his solution was not to give them up but to hide them: “I concealed my pleasures”; “a profound duplicity of life”. Hyde is the way to keep both.

**Utterson's first thought.** When he suspects blackmail, when he reads the will, when he finds Hyde's body, he thinks of his friend's name. In Chapter 8 he tells Poole they may at least save his credit.

**Everyone's first thought.** The child's family take a hundred pounds, and Enfield and the doctor threaten to make Hyde's name stink from one end of London to the other. The threat that works on a gentleman is scandal.

**The irony.** Reputation is what makes the secret necessary, and the secret is what destroys the man.

steps.body: The June 2024 indicative content named setting at nighttime, imagery of darkness, and the metaphor of the labyrinthine city as methods for fear and danger. Here is how the setting carries the themes.

steps.title: Religion and sin
steps.body:
The novel's language keeps returning to God and the devil. Hyde has “if ever I read Satan’s signature upon a face, it is on that of your new friend” on his face; Jekyll calls himself “I am the chief of sinners, I am the chief of sufferers also”; Utterson and Enfield at the window say “God forgive us, God forgive us”.

**Sin, not only crime.** Jekyll's statement reads like a confession. He speaks of temptation, of a perennial war among his members, of a self he could not govern. For a Victorian reader brought up on the Bible, the story of a man who divides himself to sin without guilt is a story about the soul.

**Science against religion.** Jekyll's transcendental science claims to do what religion said only God could: to separate good from evil in a man. The novel's ending suggests he was wrong.

visuals.alt: A table of three lines with religious language and the sense each carries

check.prompt: Jekyll calls himself the chief of sinners. Why is religious language useful for an answer on duality?
check.solution: The phrase comes from St Paul, who called himself the chief of sinners. Jekyll uses it in Chapter 6. The religious frame makes his experiment a temptation as well as a discovery.

options: Because Jekyll was a clergyman before he became a doctor, and he preached a sermon about sin every Sunday in the church near Utterson's house, which is how Utterson knew him
It frames the divided self as a matter of sin and the soul, not only of chemistry
Because Hyde goes to church

steps.title: Plan a theme answer on secrecy
steps.body:
Take a question in the exam's shape: *Starting with this extract, explore how Stevenson presents secrecy.* Imagine the extract is the end of Chapter 1, Enfield and Utterson agreeing never to refer to the story again. Plan in five lines.

1. The idea: secrecy is the gentleman's code, and it makes Hyde possible.
2. In the extract: the bargain; Queer Street.
3. Elsewhere: sealed documents.
4. Elsewhere: the form of the novel.
5. One sentence of context: the respectability of a Victorian professional man.

Then write the paragraph on the form.

steps.title: Themes that feed each other
steps.body:
A top-level answer shows how the ideas connect rather than listing them.

**Reputation makes secrecy.** A respectable man must hide what he wants.

**Secrecy makes duality.** A hidden life is a second self, and Jekyll's science gives it a body.

**Science makes it uncontrollable.** The drug works by an accident he never understood; the second self grows until it takes over.

**Setting carries all of it.** The two-faced building, the bright street and the foggy slum, the city at night.

**The claim.** *Stevenson presents duality not as good against evil but as the product of a society that forces a man to hide half of himself.*

visuals.alt: A flow chart of how the themes feed each other: reputation leads to secrecy, secrecy to duality given a body, and that to science out of control

check.prompt: Which claim about duality is conceptualised in the way the top level rewards?

steps.title: The themes in one page
steps.body:
Duality, secrecy, science, reputation: four themes, one chain.

- **Duality:** man is truly two; incongruous faggots; polar twins; the building, the city, the society.
- **Secrecy:** the bargain never to refer to it; Queer Street; sealed papers; the truth kept to the end.
- **Science:** Lanyon's material, Jekyll's transcendental; the impure salt; the proof that kills.
- **Reputation:** concealed pleasures; save his credit; the name needs the secret.
- **Setting:** a bright street and a sinister door; fog like a pall; a drowned city.
- **Religion:** Satan's signature; the chief of sinners; God forgive us.

questions.prompt: Write one analytical paragraph on how Stevenson uses setting to create an atmosphere of fear and danger.
questions.solution: Stevenson's London is a double city, and its doubleness is where the fear lives. In Chapter 1 the bright street shines “like a fire in a forest”, and in it stands “a certain sinister block of building” with a door “blistered and distained”: the neglect sits inside prosperity, as Hyde sits inside Jekyll. When Hyde kills, the city becomes a dream of evil. Fog lies over it like “A great chocolate-coloured pall lowered over heaven”, a funeral cloth, and Soho is “like a district of some city in a nightmare”, so that the reader sees respectable London turned strange. By Chapter 5 “The fog still slept on the wing above the drowned city”, and the personification of the fog as a sleeping creature and the city as drowned make the whole place seem to have sunk under the secret. On the last night even the moon is disordered: “a pale moon, lying on her back as though the wind had tilted her”. The effect is an atmosphere in which danger could be anywhere, because the city itself hides and distorts. The setting carries the novel's idea: London, like its gentlemen, has a bright face and a hidden one.

questions.prompt: Write one analytical paragraph on how Stevenson presents duality through Jekyll's statement in Chapter 10.
questions.solution: Jekyll states the novel's idea directly, “man is not truly one, but truly two”, and his images make duality a violence done to nature. The good and evil in him are “that these incongruous faggots were thus bound together”, sticks bundled against their grain, and “these polar twins should be continuously struggling”, opposites forced into one body. The antithesis in his sentences, one and two, good and evil, public and private, gives the idea the shape of a divided self. Yet his account undermines itself. He admits that before any drug he “I concealed my pleasures”, and that the drug was “neither diabolical nor divine”: it did not create evil but released “the brute that slept within me”. The duality, then, was made less by nature than by the life he chose to lead, a respectable front and a hidden pleasure. Stevenson lets Jekyll explain himself in the language of science and religion, and lets the reader see what he will not: that the divided man was divided by the need to keep his name.

examTechnique.body:
**Name the theme as a claim.** Duality made by concealment; secrecy as the gentleman's code.

**Connect themes.** Reputation, secrecy, duality, science.

**Use setting and structure as methods.** The two-faced building and city; the truth kept to the end.

**Context tied to a line.** Darwin and ape-like; respectability and Queer Street.
examinerErrors: Treating duality as simply good Jekyll against evil Hyde.
Describing Victorian London in a paragraph with no line from the novel.
Forgetting that setting is a method with an effect.
Misplacing lines: the drowned city is Chapter 5, not the last night.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer turns a theme into a claim and proves it across the novel through setting, structure and character. It shows how reputation produces secrecy and secrecy produces the divided self, reads Jekyll's statement critically, and ties context to a line. Quotations are exact and placed in the right chapter.
